FINAL HYPOTHESIS (answer)

Among individuals who were ever incarcerated (ever_jailed == 1, jailed between 1985 and 1994; n=289), median composite wealth in 1985 shows clear demographic disparities:

1. RACE — a White-vs-minority gap in median wealth. Ever-incarcerated White respondents had the highest 1985 median wealth ($2,200), versus Black ($320) and Hispanic ($0) ever-incarcerated respondents. Minority ever-incarcerated individuals thus held roughly one-seventh (Black) to effectively no (Hispanic) median wealth relative to White, and 43% (Black) and 48% (Hispanic) of them held zero or negative net wealth in 1985 (vs 23% of White). The White-vs-minority gap is robust: after removing the 1,899 duplicate rows, White stays at $2,200 while Black and Hispanic medians rise but remain well below ($1,030 and $1,380 respectively). The Black-vs-Hispanic ordering is NOT robust to duplicate handling (as-supplied: Black > Hispanic; deduped: Black < Hispanic), so only "minorities < White" should be asserted firmly.

2. SEX — ever-incarcerated women had $0 median wealth vs $1,000 for men, driven by a 65% zero-wealth share among jailed women (vs 36% for jailed men). However, female ever-jailed cells are very small (n=9–16 per race/sex cell; n=37 total), so this is indicative, not precise.

3. INCARCERATION CONTEXT — within every race-by-sex group, ever-incarcerated respondents had considerably lower 1985 median wealth than never-incarcerated respondents of the same demographic group (e.g., Hispanic men $700 vs $5,000; White men $2,000 vs $5,500; Black men $800 vs $1,500; White women $4,100 vs $5,879).

These are ASSOCIATIONS describing the 1985 wealth of a cohort ever jailed 1985–1994, not causal effects: wealth was measured in 1985 while jailing events could occur any time through 1994, and many respondents were jailed after wealth was measured. Sensitivity (as-supplied vs deduplicated; median over all values vs positive-only median $5,600) does not change the central White-vs-minority gap finding.

payload.hypothesis: Among individuals ever incarcerated (ever_jailed==1; jailed 1985-1994, n=289), median composite wealth in 1985 is much lower for Black ($320) and Hispanic ($0) than for White ($2,200) respondents, with 43-48% of minority incarcerated individuals holding zero or negative wealth; the White-vs-minority gap persists after deduplication (White $2,200 vs Black $1,030 vs Hispanic $1,380) though the Black-vs-Hispanic ordering is not robust. Ever-incarcerated women had $0 median wealth vs $1,000 for men (indicative, small cells). Within every race-by-sex group, ever-incarcerated respondents had far lower median wealth than never-incarcerated respondents of the same group. These are associations (1985 wealth of a cohort ever jailed by 1994), not causal effects.
payload.workflow: Filtered NLSY dataset to ever_jailed==1 (n=289). Computed median composite_wealth_1985 over all observed values (zeros/negatives included) by race, sex, and race x sex, with mean/zero-share/positive-only-median, deduplicated sensitivity (n=239), and never-jailed reference medians per demographic group. All outputs in analysis_outputs.json; full tables in analysis log.
